\chapter{Integrated Likelihood Inference}\label{ch:methodology}

\section{Overview}

The preceding chapter established the integrated likelihood as a
principled approach to eliminating nuisance parameters from inference,
provided an appropriate weight function can be identified. This chapter
develops a general computational procedure for approximating the
integrated likelihood in models where the nuisance parameter is
high-dimensional and the integration cannot be carried out in closed
form. The procedure is built on the zero-score-expectation (ZSE)
parameterization of @severini2007 and @severini2018, which provides a
canonical choice of weight function with favorable frequentist
properties. Subsequent chapters specialize this general procedure to
specific models and parameters of interest.

Throughout this chapter we work with a generic model parameterized by
$\theta \in \Theta$ and a scalar parameter of interest
$\psi = \varphi(\theta)$ for some function $\varphi: \Theta \to
\mathbbm{R}$. We denote the unrestricted MLE by $\hat{\theta}$, the
induced MLE for $\psi$ by $\hat{\psi} = \varphi(\hat{\theta})$, and the
constrained parameter space at a fixed value of $\psi$ by
$\Theta(\psi) = \{\theta \in \Theta : \varphi(\theta) = \psi\}$.

\section{The Zero-Score Expectation Parameterization}

\subsection{Explicit nuisance parameters}

@severini2007 considered the problem of selecting a weight function
$\pi(\lambda \mid \psi)$ for the integrated likelihood
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_\Lambda L(\psi, \lambda)\, \pi(\lambda \mid \psi)\, d\lambda
$$
such that the resulting integrated likelihood possesses well-defined
frequentist properties. He showed that a suitable weight function can be
constructed by identifying a reparameterization $(\psi, \lambda)
\mapsto (\psi, \phi)$ of the nuisance parameter with the property that
$\hat{\phi}_\psi = \hat{\phi}$ --- that is, the conditional MLE of
$\phi$ given $\psi$ equals its unrestricted MLE --- and then choosing a
prior $\pi(\phi)$ that does not depend on $\psi$. An integrated
likelihood with the desired properties is then
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_\Phi \tilde{L}(\psi, \phi)\, \pi(\phi)\, d\phi,
$${#eq-ZSE-IL-explicit}
where $\tilde{L}(\psi, \phi)$ is the likelihood after reparameterization.
The specific choice of $\pi(\phi)$ is secondary; the key requirement is
that it not depend on $\psi$.

The reparameterization is achieved by defining $\phi$ as the solution to
$$
\mathrm{E}_{(\psi_0, \lambda_0)}\!\left[\nabla_\lambda\,
\ell(\psi, \lambda;\, \mathbf{X}_n)\right]
\Bigg|_{(\psi_0,\, \lambda_0)\,=\,(\hat{\psi},\, \phi)} = \mathbf{0},
$${#eq-ZSE-condition}
where the expectation is taken with respect to the data distribution
evaluated at the true parameter values $(\psi_0, \lambda_0) =
(\hat{\psi}, \phi)$. The quantity $\phi$ is called the
\emph{zero-score-expectation parameter} because it is defined as the
nuisance value at which the expected score for $\lambda$ vanishes. Since
$\phi$ satisfies @eq-ZSE-condition for a given $(\psi, \lambda,
\hat{\psi})$, it is implicitly a function of the data through $\hat{\psi}$.
Once $\phi$ is determined, the corresponding nuisance parameter value
is recovered as
$$
\lambda(\psi, \phi) = \underset{\lambda \in \Lambda}{\mathrm{argmax}}\;
\mathrm{E}_{(\hat{\psi},\, \phi)}\!\left[\ell(\psi, \lambda;\,
\mathbf{X}_n)\right],
$${#eq-ZSE-lambda}
and @eq-ZSE-IL-explicit can be written entirely in terms of the
original parameterization:
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_\Phi L\!\left(\psi,\, \lambda(\psi, \phi)\right)
\pi(\phi)\, d\phi.
$${#eq-ZSE-IL-explicit2}

\subsection{Implicit nuisance parameters}

@severini2018 extended the ZSE construction to settings where $\psi$ is
an implicit function of a single model parameter $\theta$, with no
explicit separation into interest and nuisance components. In this
setting, the role of the ZSE nuisance value $\phi$ is played by a point
$\omega$ on the level set
$$
\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} = \left\{\omega \in \Theta : \varphi(\omega) =
\hat{\psi}\right\},
$${#eq-level-set}
and @eq-ZSE-lambda generalizes to
$$
\theta^*(\psi, \omega) = \underset{\varphi(\theta)\,=\,\psi}{\mathrm{argmax}}\;
\mathrm{E}_\omega\!\left[\ell(\theta;\, \mathbf{X}_n)\right].
$${#eq-ZSE-theta}
The integrated likelihood for $\psi$ is then
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}} L\!\left(\theta^*(\psi, \omega)
\right) \pi(\omega)\, d\omega,
$${#eq-ZSE-IL-implicit}
where $\pi(\omega)$ is a density on $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ that does not
depend on $\psi$. The expression in @eq-ZSE-IL-implicit is the
central object of interest in this paper.

\section{Branches and the Profile Likelihood}

\subsection{Branch functions}

The integrand in @eq-ZSE-IL-implicit assigns to each $\omega \in
\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ a likelihood value $L(\theta^*(\psi, \omega))$,
obtained by evaluating the likelihood at the parameter value
$\theta^*(\psi, \omega)$ that maximizes the expected log-likelihood
subject to $\varphi(\theta) = \psi$. We refer to the function
$$
b(\psi;\, \omega) = L\!\left(\theta^*(\psi, \omega)\right),
\quad \psi \in \Psi,
$${#eq-branch-fn}
as the \emph{branch function} associated with $\omega$. Each $\omega
\in \Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ induces a distinct branch function, and the
integrated likelihood is the average of these branch functions over the
level set:
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}} b(\psi;\, \omega)\,
\pi(\omega)\, d\omega.
$${#eq-IL-branches}
The profile likelihood is the special case in which $\omega =
\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ --- the point on $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$
induced by the unrestricted MLE --- and the expected log-likelihood
reduces to the observed log-likelihood. In this case $\theta^*(\psi,
\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) = \hat{\theta}(\psi)$, the constrained
MLE at $\psi$, and $b(\psi;\, \hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) =
L_P(\psi)$ is the profile likelihood. The integrated likelihood can
therefore be interpreted as a weighted average of profile-like
likelihood curves, each anchored at a different point on the level set.

\subsection{The branch mode}

For a given $\omega$, the branch function $b(\psi;\, \omega)$ has a
maximum over $\psi \in \Psi$, which we call the \emph{branch mode}:
$$
\psi^*(\omega) = \underset{\psi \in \Psi}{\mathrm{argmax}}\;
b(\psi;\, \omega).
$${#eq-branch-mode}
The branch mode is the value of $\psi$ at which the likelihood is
highest along the constrained path parametrized by $\omega$. For the
profile likelihood branch, $\psi^*(\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) =
\hat{\psi}$ by construction. For other branches the mode may differ from
$\hat{\psi}$, reflecting the fact that different nuisance configurations
are compatible with different values of the parameter of interest.

\section{Monte Carlo Approximation}

\subsection{The approximation problem}

Direct evaluation of @eq-IL-branches requires integration over
$\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$, which is a manifold of dimension $\dim(\Theta) -
1$ in general. In high-dimensional models this integration is
intractable, and we instead approximate it by a Monte Carlo average over
a finite collection of $\omega$ values sampled from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$:
$$
\bar{L}(\psi) \approx \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^R b(\psi;\, \omega^{(r)}),
$${#eq-IL-MC}
where $\omega^{(1)}, \dots, \omega^{(R)}$ are draws from a distribution
supported on $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$. The quality of the approximation
depends on (i) how densely and representatively the draws cover the
level set and (ii) whether the branch functions associated with the
drawn $\omega$ values are well-behaved.

\subsection{Sampling omega-hat values}

Sampling from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ proceeds in two stages. First, an
initial candidate in the ambient parameter space $\Theta$ is generated
by perturbing the MLE $\hat{\theta}$ in directions tangent to the level
set. Second, the candidate is projected onto $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ by
solving a constrained feasibility problem with respect to $\psi$. The
projection does not optimize the likelihood; it simply finds a feasible
point consistent with the observed $\hat{\psi}$. The design of the
initial generator is problem-specific and is discussed in detail for
each model in the chapters that follow.

\subsection{Evaluating branch functions}

For each sampled $\omega^{(r)}$, the branch function $b(\psi;\,
\omega^{(r)})$ is evaluated over a grid of $\psi$ values. At each grid
point $\psi_k$, the branch value is computed by solving
@eq-ZSE-theta --- maximizing the expected log-likelihood subject to the
constraint $\varphi(\theta) = \psi_k$ --- and evaluating the likelihood
at the resulting $\theta^*(\psi_k, \omega^{(r)})$. Solutions are chained
across the grid: the optimizer at $\psi_k$ is initialized from the
solution at $\psi_{k-1}$, exploiting the continuity of $\theta^*(\psi;\,
\omega)$ in $\psi$.

Before tracing a branch across the full grid, the algorithm first
locates the branch mode $\psi^*(\omega^{(r)})$ via a one-dimensional
search. The branch is then traced outward in both directions from the
mode until the branch value falls below a threshold determined by the
confidence levels of interest.

\subsection{Branch screening}

Not all sampled $\omega$ values yield well-behaved branch functions. A
branch is considered valid if it has a unique interior mode, decreases
monotonically on each side of the mode, and does not exhibit
discontinuities or anomalous curvature. Draws that fail these criteria
are discarded before the integrated likelihood is assembled. This
screening step can be interpreted as a regularization of the integration
measure: by restricting attention to well-behaved nuisance
configurations, the approximation is made more stable at the cost of a
slight bias in the weight function. The specific screening criteria are
discussed in the context of each model in the chapters that follow.

\subsection{Assembling the integrated likelihood}

Valid branch functions are evaluated on a common $\psi$ grid and
averaged pointwise to form the integrated likelihood approximation
@eq-IL-MC. The profile likelihood is constructed from the single branch
corresponding to $\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ and provides a baseline
for comparison. Confidence intervals for $\psi$ are obtained by
inverting the likelihood ratio statistic against both the integrated and
profile likelihoods, using the standard $\chi^2_1$ reference
distribution.

\section{The Two-Space Problem}\label{sec:two-space}

A structural subtlety arises in regression models where the level set
$\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ lives in a different space from the model
parameter $\theta$. In the no-effects model, $\theta = \symbf{\theta}
\in \Delta^{J-1}$ and $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \subset \Delta^{J-1}$, so
$\omega$ and $\theta$ inhabit the same space and the branch construction
is straightforward. In regression models, $\theta$ is a matrix of
regression coefficients while $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a manifold of
probability vectors at a reference covariate value $\symbf{x}_0$.

Bridging this gap requires a map from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \subset
\Delta^{J-1}$ to $\Theta$. The construction used throughout this paper
is a rank-one adjustment of the MLE that matches the linear predictor at
$\symbf{x}_0$ to the logit vector implied by $\omega$, while leaving the
regression coefficients unchanged in all directions orthogonal to
$\symbf{x}_0$. The specific form of this adjustment and its consequences
for the alignment between the surrogate and true log-likelihoods are
discussed in the context of each model.
